## Chapter Summary

A query is a written request for data that the database answers where the data is stored. Querying suits an accounting analysis when the data is large, when it spans related tables, and when the procedure must be repeated. The query text itself documents what was extracted, so it can be reviewed and run again. SQL is the standard language of relational databases, and it is declarative: you state the result you want, and the database decides how to produce it. This book uses SQLite, which keeps a whole database in one file, and DB Browser for SQLite, whose Database Structure tab shows every table and column and whose Execute SQL tab runs queries. Because DB Browser can change a database as well as read it, you work in a copy of the download, CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite. Write Changes stays grayed out while you only read.

A SELECT statement is built from clauses that name the columns it wants and the table they come from. A syntax error, such as a misspelled column, stops the statement, and the red message pane names the problem. Aliases rename columns in the result, and calculated columns apply arithmetic to each row, with ROUND keeping amounts to the cent. Two whole numbers divide as whole numbers, so a ratio of counts needs a decimal. Scalar functions return one value for each row. ABS removes a sign, CAST converts a value to another type, SUBSTR takes a code apart, and UPPER, TRIM, and REPLACE standardize text. DISTINCT lists the values a column actually holds, which is the way to learn the valid values before you filter on one.

The WHERE clause keeps the rows that meet a condition, built from comparison operators, BETWEEN, IN, and LIKE, and combined with AND, OR, and NOT. Text values sit in single quotes and must match the data exactly. SQLite converts a value to the type of the column it is compared with, but it never converts when neither side is a column, so text compared with a number finds nothing. Dates stored as text are compared with dates written the same way, and a column that also stores a time needs a range that ends before the next day. Parentheses make the order of AND and OR explicit. A missing value is NULL, which no comparison can match, so IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the tests for it, and COALESCE replaces it with a value you choose.

ORDER BY sorts a result by one or more columns or expressions, and LIMIT keeps its first rows. Together they rank transactions, such as the largest variances of a year. A script saved from the Execute SQL tab keeps a chapter's queries together, with a header comment that records their purpose, source, preparer, and checks. Copy with Headers moves a result into Excel, and Export to CSV writes it to a file. Logical errors, such as a missing comma or a text value compared with a number, return a result that answers the wrong question. The defense against them is to know what the result should look like before running the query.

Applied to the controller's question, the queries showed that the manufacturing variance is recorded when work orders close, and that the variance parts of every close add up to its total. They also showed that the ledger postings of fiscal 2026 must be separated from the closing entry that clears the account. In the largest closes of the year, overhead makes up most of the variance, and the favorable closes are fewer and smaller than the unfavorable ones. Which products carry the variance and how it grew from year to year are questions for Chapter 10.
